meta.title: Who really said "That Works Very Well in Practice, But How Does It Work In Theory?"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Garret FitzGerald. Quote Investigator traces the joke to an anonymous 1911 anecdote; it was first put in FitzGerald's mouth in 1985, by an impersonator.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'That Works Very Well in Practice, But How Does It Work In Theory?'?
meta.ogDescription: The joke about economists predates Garret FitzGerald by more than seventy years. Its earliest strong match is an unsigned 1911 magazine filler about a professor.

answer.label: Not Garret FitzGerald — an anonymous joke
answer.authorDates: Origin anonymous · earliest strong match 1911 · attached to FitzGerald only from 1985
answer.sourceLine: This is a long-running joke about economists, not a FitzGerald original. Quote Investigator ↗ traces its earliest strong match to an unsigned 1911 magazine anecdote about a Heidelberg professor and concludes that the originator was anonymous, with later instances popularised by W. R. Rodgers, Claude T. Bissell, Sean MacReamoinn and Walter Heller. FitzGerald enters the story only in 1985, when the businessman Tony O’Reilly put a version of the line in his mouth during a comic impersonation — and his 2011 obituary in The New York Times then reported it as something FitzGerald had actually said.

source.heading: The 1985 moment the line became ‘his’

docMeta.dd: The Irish Times, 6 July 1985 — reporting an impersonation, not a speech

source.excerpt: “That’s a very good idea,” said Garret. “I know it will work very well in practice, but tell me John, how will it work in theory?”
trail: 1911 — the earliest strong match located by Quote Investigator ↗ is an unsigned filler item, “A Professional Paradox,” in The Youth’s Companion of 5 October 1911. A Heidelberg professor forbids an experiment that has always succeeded: “The thing may answer very well in practise, but it is not sound in theory.”

1951 & 1959 — the modern shape arrives. W. R. Rodgers, writing in The New Statesman and Nation of 6 January 1951, tells of an Irish company chairman greeting record dividends with “this is all very well in practice. But how does it work out in theory?” Claude T. Bissell, president of the University of Toronto, retold the same Irish-boardroom story in Varsity Graduate, volume 8 (1959) ↗.

1979 — the joke is recast as a definition of economists and credited to Walter W. Heller, adviser to Presidents Kennedy and Johnson. Barry Popik ↗ collects the newspaper run from the Seattle Daily Times of 4 July 1979 onward; FitzGerald appears nowhere in it.

1985 → 2011 — Tony O’Reilly’s impersonation puts the line in FitzGerald’s mouth, and FitzGerald’s New York Times obituary of 20 May 2011 reports a version of it as his own remark. Quote Investigator ↗ documents both, and still concludes the originator was anonymous.
source.excerptNote: This is not Garret FitzGerald speaking. It is Tony O’Reilly performing FitzGerald — sketching an imaginary cabinet meeting in which John Bruton, then a minister in FitzGerald’s government, proposes a solution to the balance of payments problem. The Irish Times reported the routine on 6 July 1985 and noted the audience laughed. It is the earliest connection between this joke and FitzGerald that anyone has documented, and it is a joke about him, not by him.

source.rightsNote: No rights status can honestly be asserted, because the popular wording has no identifiable author or first publication. The 1911 anecdote that supplies the joke’s earliest strong match is unsigned and long out of copyright, but it uses different words; the wordings that most resemble the modern form appear in works still under copyright — The New Statesman and Nation (1951), The Irish Times (1985) and The New York Times (2011). The exact string usually quoted matches none of them.

author.name: Garret FitzGerald
author.kicker: The man the joke landed on
author.heading: Why it stuck to him
author.metaLine: 1926–2011 · Taoiseach of Ireland and academic economist
author.bio: Garret FitzGerald (9 February 1926 – 19 May 2011) was a Fine Gael politician who served two terms as Taoiseach, from June 1981 to March 1982 and from December 1982 to March 1987. Before politics he built a career in economics — working in transport planning at Aer Lingus, acting as Irish correspondent for The Economist, lecturing at University College Dublin and taking a UCD doctorate in economics in 1968, published as Planning in Ireland. That combination — a working economist running a country, with a public reputation for professorial abstraction — is precisely what made him a plausible host for a joke that had been circulating, unowned, for decades before he reached office.

cite.sourceCitation: “A Professional Paradox.” The Youth’s Companion: For All the Family 85, no. 40 (October 5, 1911): 515 — the earliest strong match located by Quote Investigator, which concludes the quip’s originator was anonymous. The line was first attached to Garret FitzGerald in Anthony O’Reilly’s comic impersonation of him, reported in The Irish Times (Dublin), July 6, 1985, 14.

copyAttribution: Not Garret FitzGerald. The joke is anonymous: Quote Investigator's earliest strong match is an unsigned 1911 item, "A Professional Paradox," in The Youth's Companion (5 October 1911), and it concludes the originator cannot be identified. Close matches follow in The New Statesman and Nation (1951), Varsity Graduate (1959), The Irish Times (1972) and The Washington Star (1979, credited to economist Walter W. Heller). FitzGerald was first linked to the line on 6 July 1985, when The Irish Times reported Tony O'Reilly delivering it as part of a comic impersonation of him; his New York Times obituary of 20 May 2011 then printed a version as FitzGerald's own remark.

misattribution.heading: Everyone this joke has been pinned on
misattribution.intro: This is a travelling gag, not a quotation. It attaches itself to whichever public figure best fits the caricature of the theorist, and the record shows it changing hosts roughly once a decade.

items.scope: “That’s fine in practice, but will it work in theory?”
items.why: The earliest FitzGerald instance found by Quote Investigator ↗ is The Irish Times of 6 July 1985, reporting Tony O’Reilly giving “a superb imitation of Garret FitzGerald” and sketching an imaginary cabinet meeting in which FitzGerald’s minister John Bruton proposes a fix for the balance of payments. The words are O’Reilly’s comic invention. FitzGerald’s 2011 obituary in The New York Times later printed a version as his own line, and quote aggregators have repeated it since with no source at all ↗.

items.scope: “An economist is someone who says, when an idea works in practice, ‘let’s see if it works in theory.’”
items.why: Credited to the former chairman of the US Council of Economic Advisers in The Washington Star of 28 June 1979, per Quote Investigator ↗, and repeated in newspapers through the 1980s as collected by Barry Popik ↗. The joke was already in print decades before he used it, and Quote Investigator concludes the originator was anonymous.

items.scope: “Economist: Someone who finds something in practice and wonders if it will work in theory.”
items.why: Attributed to the US senator in The Plain Dealer of Cleveland on 8 May 1988, as documented by Quote Investigator ↗ — nine years after the Heller version was already in print.

items.who: W. R. Rodgers, Claude T. Bissell and Sean MacReamoinn
items.why: Rodgers told it in The New Statesman and Nation in January 1951 about an unnamed Irish company chairman; Bissell retold the same story in the University of Toronto’s Varsity Graduate, volume 8 (1959) ↗; MacReamoinn was quoting it on Irish radio by 1972. Quote Investigator ↗ names all three as popularisers, not originators.

misattribution.truthLine: Quote Investigator’s conclusion ↗ is explicit: “this quip evolved over many decades, and its originator was anonymous.” Garret FitzGerald is one of the later names it was handed to — and the only one who got it by way of a comedian doing an impression of him.

context.heading: How a joke about economists found a Taoiseach
lead: The gag works by inverting a sturdy old complaint. “That’s fine in theory, but will it work in practice?” is the ordinary sceptic’s objection; reversing it produces an instant caricature of the theorist who cannot accept good news until the model agrees. That is why it has been handed round for a century, landing on whoever the era’s most conspicuous theorist happened to be — a Heidelberg professor in 1911, an Irish company chairman in 1951, a university president’s alumni-magazine essay in 1959, an economic adviser to two US presidents in 1979.

Garret FitzGerald was an unusually good fit. He was a doctorate-holding economist who became head of government, and his public image ran to the professorial. When Tony O’Reilly wanted a laugh at a 1985 event, doing FitzGerald chairing a cabinet meeting, the line was already sitting there waiting. The impersonation is the point: O’Reilly was not reporting something FitzGerald said, he was writing a joke in FitzGerald’s voice. Twenty-six years later, an obituary printed a version of it as FitzGerald’s own remark, and the loop closed.
context.detailsSummary: One more wrinkle: the wording everybody quotes isn’t in any of the sources
detailsBody: Compare the documented wordings and none of them is the popular form. 1951 gives “this is all very well in practice. But how does it work out in theory?”; 1959, “That is all very well in practice, but how will it work out in theory?”; 1972, “It’s all very well in practice. How is it in theory?”; the 1985 O’Reilly impersonation, “I know it will work very well in practice, but tell me John, how will it work in theory?”; the 2011 obituary, “That’s fine in practice, but will it work in theory?”

The string circulating today — “That Works Very Well in Practice, But How Does It Work In Theory?” — is in fact the headline of Quote Investigator’s 2015 article ↗ on the subject. That is a researcher’s summary of a family of jokes, not a sentence anyone is recorded as speaking. It is worth saying plainly, because a quotation that exists only in its investigator’s title is about as far from a sourced utterance as a quotation can get.
context.pull: The line was never FitzGerald’s. It was O’Reilly’s — doing FitzGerald.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator concludes the quip's originator was anonymous; its earliest strong match is 'A Professional Paradox' in The Youth's Companion, 5 October 1911, vol. 85 no. 40, p. 515; it documents close matches in The New Statesman and Nation (6 Jan 1951, W. R. Rodgers), Varsity Graduate (Sept 1959, Claude T. Bissell), The Irish Times (4 July 1972, Sean MacReamoinn), The Washington Star (28 June 1979, Walter W. Heller) and The Plain Dealer (8 May 1988, Ernest Hollings); and links FitzGerald only via The Irish Times of 6 July 1985 (Tony O'Reilly's impersonation, quoted verbatim) and his New York Times obituary of 20 May 2011.
Barry Popik documents the 'an economist is someone who...' form from the Seattle Daily Times of 4 July 1979 onward, associates it primarily with Walter Heller, and does not mention Garret FitzGerald.

Garret FitzGerald was born 9 February 1926 and died 19 May 2011; he was Taoiseach 30 June 1981 - 9 March 1982 and 14 December 1982 - 10 March 1987; he worked at Aer Lingus, was Irish correspondent for The Economist, lectured in economics at UCD and took a UCD PhD in economics in 1968, published as 'Planning in Ireland'; he was Fine Gael. The article does not contain the practice/theory quip.
The scanned item is Varsity Graduate, volume 8, published 1959 by the Department of Information, University of Toronto - the volume Quote Investigator cites for Claude T. Bissell's retelling.
The quote 'That's fine in practice, but will it work in theory?' circulates on Goodreads attributed to Garret FitzGerald with no source or citation given.

Sir Anthony John Francis O'Reilly (7 May 1936 - 18 May 2024) was an Irish businessman who led the Independent News & Media Group from 1973 to 2009 - i.e. the 'A.J.F. O'Reilly' / newspaper magnate named in the 1985 Irish Times item.
John Bruton was a member of Garret FitzGerald's cabinet in 1985, serving as Minister for Industry, Trade, Commerce and Tourism from 13 December 1983 to 14 February 1986.
